title: Globular Cluster Omega Centauri Captured by NEWFIRM on the Blanco Telescope
caption: The globular cluster Omega Centauri, imaged by NEWFIRM on the Blanco 4-meter Telescope
credit: CTIO/NOIRLab/DOE/NSF/AURA, T.A. Rector (University of Alaska Anchorage/NSF NOIRLab), M. Zamani & D. de Martin (NSF NOIRLab)

recognition.text: Image from an NSF NOIRLab announcement. No published audience rating.

story: This infrared image shows Omega Centauri, the largest globular cluster in the Milky Way, packed with approximately 10 million stars. Seen toward the constellation Centaurus, it is about 17,000 light-years from Earth.

NEWFIRM, an infrared camera on Cerro Tololo Inter-American Observatory's Víctor M. Blanco 4-meter Telescope in Chile, recorded the cluster while it was being commissioned and put through capability tests. Its size and richness make Omega Centauri a popular target for such observations.

A globular cluster is a dense, roughly spherical swarm of old stars bound together by gravity. Observing in infrared light has particular advantages for a cluster like this. Infrared passes through dust more easily than visible light, and many of the cool, old stars that fill globular clusters shine strongly at these longer wavelengths. Testing a new camera on such a crowded field also shows how well it can separate stars packed close together.
scale: Omega Centauri is about 17,000 light-years from Earth, according to NOIRLab.

understand.summary: NEWFIRM on the Blanco 4-meter Telescope observed Omega Centauri in near-infrared light through J, H and Ks filters. The colors assigned to each filter are not published.
